answer:
**These techniques reduce different parts of tree-training cost.** GOSS reduces which training rows contribute to split estimation, EFB reduces effective feature representation for suitable sparse features, and leaf-wise growth changes which node is expanded next. They should not be treated as three names for one optimization. [1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2017/hash/6449f44a102fde848669bdd9eb6b76fa-Abstract.html)

**GOSS intuition.** Examples with large gradients indicate current difficulty, so keep more of them while sampling smaller-gradient examples and correcting their contribution. This attempts to save work without discarding the most informative current errors. The sampling/reweighting details matter for the resulting split estimates.

**EFB intuition.** If sparse features rarely take nonzero values together, they can be bundled with bookkeeping that preserves their identity. This reduces the number of separate feature structures processed. Strong overlap weakens the premise; arbitrary dense features cannot simply be merged without consequences.

**Growth policy changes capacity allocation.** Depth-wise growth expands a level broadly. Leaf-wise best-first growth selects the leaf offering the greatest current gain, potentially producing a deep uneven tree. That can fit efficiently but needs leaf-count, depth, and minimum-data constraints to avoid overfitting small regions.

Modern implementations have overlapping features and configurable policies, so avoid equating a library name permanently with one growth rule. Benchmark the actual version/configuration on representative data, including memory, training time, missing/categorical handling, and validation quality.

**Technical details and references.**

GOSS retains large-gradient examples and subsamples small-gradient ones with reweighting, targeting examples that strongly influence split gain. EFB bundles sparse, nearly mutually exclusive features to reduce effective dimensionality. Leaf-wise growth splits the currently most promising leaf; depth-wise growth expands a level more uniformly. [1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2017/hash/6449f44a102fde848669bdd9eb6b76fa-Abstract.html)

Best-first growth can reduce training loss with fewer leaves but may create deep, specialized branches and overfit small datasets. Limit leaves, depth, and minimum leaf data. XGBoost also supports multiple growth/histogram strategies, so “LightGBM leaf-wise, XGBoost always depth-wise” is outdated as a universal distinction. [2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.02754)

Compare actual configurations, categorical handling, memory, training time, and held-out quality. Neither GOSS nor EFB guarantees a speedup or quality match on dense or highly interacting features.
